subject: Architecture
title: Car-Free Urban Design
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Car-Free Urban Design.

hook.text: Roads and parking consume 30-60% of urban land. What if cities gave all that space back to people?

buildup.text: Car-free zones in Amsterdam, Copenhagen, and Ghent have increased foot traffic, revenue, and quality of life.

discovery.text: Oslo removed all parking from its city center. Shops feared ruin — but sales actually increased by 10%.

twist.text: Autonomous vehicles could eliminate the need for parking altogether — cars drop you off and leave.

climax.text: Saudi Arabia's NEOM/The Line proposes a 105-mile linear city — no cars, no streets, just walking paths.

punchline.text: We built cities for cars. The future is building them for humans again.

quiz.question: What happened when Oslo removed parking from its city center?
options: Shops reported a 10% increase in sales
Businesses moved to the suburbs in protest
Traffic jams worsened on surrounding roads

details.summary: Car-free urban design reclaims streets for pedestrians, cyclists, and green space by eliminating or drastically reducing private vehicle access. Superblocks in Barcelona, the car-free town of Vauban in Germany, and proposed developments worldwide show that cities designed for people, not cars.
details.whyItMatters: Cars consume a third of urban land for roads and parking. Removing them reclaims vast space for housing, parks, and public life while reducing pollution, noise, and pedestrian deaths.
takeaways: Car-free design reclaims streets for people and green space
Removing cars reduces pollution, noise, and traffic deaths

faq.question: What is a superblock and how does it work?
faq.answer: Barcelona's superblocks group nine city blocks into a single unit where through-traffic is banned. Streets inside become pedestrian plazas, playgrounds, and green spaces. Cars can still access residences but cannot cut through, reducing traffic by 25% and pollution significantly.

faq.question: Can car-free design work in sprawling cities?
faq.answer: Complete car-freedom suits dense urban cores. In sprawling cities, the approach works by creating car-free zones within districts rather than eliminating cars entirely. Vauban shows that even suburban-style developments can function with minimal car ownership when transit and cycling are excellent.
